Title: Current and Future Development in Lung Cancer Diagnosis.
Abstract: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related deaths in North America and other developed countries. One of the reasons lung cancer is at the top of the list is that it is often not diagnosed until the cancer is at an advanced stage. Thus, the earliest diagnosis of lung cancer is crucial, especially in screening high-risk populations, such as smokers, exposure to fumes, oil fields, toxic occupational places, etc. Based on the current knowledge, it looks that there is an urgent need to identify novel biomarkers. The current diagnosis of lung cancer includes different types of imaging complemented with pathological assessment of biopsies, but these techniques can still not detect early lung cancer developments. In this review, we described the advantages and disadvantages of current methods used in diagnosing lung cancer, and we provide an analysis of the potential use of body fluids as carriers of biomarkers as predictors of cancer development and progression.
Abstract_Summary: Lung cancer is a sickness in the lungs. It is very common in many rich lands. Many people learn they have it very late. Late means the sickness has grown a lot. Then it is harder for doctors to help. Some people have a higher chance of lung cancer. This can include people who smoke often. It can also include people near bad fumes. Some jobs have dust, gas, or harsh stuff. These can also raise the chance of cancer. Doctors now use scans and pictures of lungs. They also take a tiny piece called a biopsy. They look at it under a strong scope. These tools help, but not always very early. The article says we need better test tools. It talks about “markers” inside our bodies. Markers are tiny signs that sickness may start. These markers may be found in body fluids. Body fluids can be blood, spit, or pee. They are easier and safer to collect. If we find good markers in these fluids, Doctors may see lung cancer much more early. Then they can plan care sooner and better. The article lists good and bad of old tests. It also shares ideas for new marker tests. The goal is to spot lung cancer much sooner. This may help many people stay more healthy.
Full_Text_Summary_With_In_Text_Citations: This research looks at better ways to find lung cancer early, before it has spread and is hard to treat (Abstract, para. 1). Today, many people learn they have lung cancer only when it is at stage 3 or 4, which leads to low 5‑year survival rates, sometimes under 5% (Body, para. 10). This work may help people at high risk, such as long‑time smokers or those exposed to toxic fumes (Introduction, para. 2). The authors review how lung cancer is now found, mainly with scans, scopes into the lung, and tissue samples, and explain why these tools often miss very small tumors and can cause pain, cost, and side effects (Body, para. 27). They then describe new lab tests that use body fluids like blood, spit, and urine to look for “biomarkers,” which are cancer‑linked signals such as bits of tumor DNA, small control molecules, or changes in normal blood cells (Conclusion, para. 3). Many of these fluid tests can tell people with lung cancer from healthy people, even in early stages, but results vary between studies and are not yet ready for wide use (Body, para. 39). The authors suggest that, in the future, simple blood or urine tests could work with lung scans to pick out who truly needs a biopsy and who does not, making early checks safer, faster, and less costly (Conclusion, para. 4).
